subject: english-literature
title: First Pass and Form
welcome_lead: Confronted with a poem you have never read, work systematically. Form, structure, voice — the first pass.
meta_desc: Unseen poetry analysis — form, structure and voice at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You have a method for the unseen poem — form first, voice second, music third.

concepts.def: The skill of closely reading a poem you have not studied before, working out its meaning, methods and effects within the time limit of an exam.
Language that appeals to the senses or creates mental pictures, including metaphor, simile and personification, which shapes a poem's mood and meaning.
The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a poem; a regular metre such as iambic pentameter creates a beat that poets may disrupt for effect.
The overall shape of a poem, including stanza length, line breaks, rhyme scheme and turning points, which guide how its meaning unfolds.
The attitude and mood conveyed by the speaker, and the identity of the speaking persona, which may differ from the poet themselves.
Enjambment runs a sentence over a line break without pause, while a caesura is a pause within a line; both control a poem's pace and emphasis.

walkthroughs.body_html: Before reading carefully, scan the visual shape. Fourteen lines suggests sonnet. Tight quatrains suggest hymn or ballad. Long irregular lines suggest free verse or modernist project.
Ask: who speaks, to whom, why? A first-person speaker addressing an absent beloved produces a love lyric. A persona speaking from history produces a dramatic monologue.
Reading aloud catches rhythm shifts, caesurae and rhyme effects that silent reading misses. Note any moment where the meter falters — it usually signals interpretive weight.

mcqs.q: When analysing an unseen poem, you should first focus on:
options: The poet's biography
The poem's meaning, methods and effects
The exam timetable
Quotes from poems you have studied
A line ends with a full stop
A sentence runs over a line break without a pause
Two poems rhyme
A stanza repeats

mcqs.q: The 'speaker' or persona of a poem:
options: Is always the poet
May be a voice distinct from the poet
Is the reader
Is the examiner

mcqs.q: A volta in a poem is a:
options: Type of rhyme
Turn or shift in argument or mood
Closing couplet only
Missing line

mcqs.q: Is the speaker of a poem always the poet?
options: Poems never have a speaker.
The 'I' in a poem is always the poet themselves.
No - the speaker is a persona who may be quite different from the poet.
When a poem has no punctuation at all.
When two lines rhyme with each other.
Poems never have a speaker.
When a sentence runs over the line break without a pause.
When a poem has no punctuation at all.

mcqs.q: How should you tackle an unseen poem in an exam?
options: Just summarise the plot of the poem.
Guess the poet and write out their biography.
Read closely for meaning, methods and effects, then build an argument.
Poems never have a speaker.
